case_name: Natco International, Inc. v. Photo Violation Technologies Corp.
text:
SUPREME COURT
OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Natco International, Inc. v. Photo
Violation Technologies Corp. and

Natco International, Inc. v. Minor,

2008 BCSC 1325

Date: 20081003

Docket:
S078417

Registry:
Vancouver

Between:

Natco International, Inc.

Plaintiffs

And

Photo Violation Technologies Corp.,

Fred Mitschele aka Fred Marlatt

Defendants

AND
:

Docket:
S081159

Registry:
Vancouver

Between:

Natco International, Inc.

Plaintiffs

And

Michael Wallace Minor, aka Mike
Minor,

Jason
Michael Joseph Mitschele, and Malisa Phoiliang

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Griffin

Reasons for Judgment

Re: Defence Application to Strike Claims

Counsel for Natco International, Inc.

R.
Shore

Counsel for Defendants Fred Mitschele,
Jason Mitschele and Malisa Phoiliang; and agents for Counsel for Photo Violation
Technologies Corp.

H.
Shapray, B. Cramer

Counsel for Defendant Michael Minor

S.
Warnett, M. Maniago

Date and Place of Hearing:

July
21-23, 2008

Vancouver,
B.C.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

Natco International Inc. (“Natco”) and Photo
Violation Technologies Corp. (“PVT”) are embroiled in three lawsuits against
each other and related directors.  The pleadings in this plethora of claims and
cross-claims are prolix.

[
2
]

The parties opposite Natco in the two actions
commenced by Natco have brought motions seeking to strike out portions of the
allegations in Natco’s statements of claim.  The basis for these applications
is twofold:

(a)       PVT argues that Natco is
precluded from suing for the loss of benefits of an alleged contract between
Natco and PVT because Natco terminated the contract and, therefore, PVT seeks
to have that portion of Natco’s claim dismissed on a summary trial basis
pursuant to Rule 18; and

(b)       the defendants say that Natco’s
statements of claim offend the rules of pleading and ought to be struck on the
grounds that they disclose no reasonable claim or, alternatively, are
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, vexatious, or may prejudice, embarrass or
delay the proceeding.  On this basis, the applicants apply to have all or
portions of Natco’s statements of claim struck out pursuant to Rule 19(24).

THE LAWSUITS

[
3
]

There are three inter-related actions arising
out of a failed commercial transaction, or series of transactions, between
Natco and PVT.  I will call the first claim Natco #1.  This is a claim by Natco
against PVT and a PVT director, Fred Mitschele, also known as Fred Marlatt,
filed as Action No. S078417, Vancouver Registry.

[
4
]

The second action, which I will call Natco #2, was
commenced by Natco against Malisa Phoiliang, Mike Minor and Jason Mitschele,
Action No. S081159, Vancouver Registry.  In Natco #2, Natco alleges that
Michael Minor, Jason Mitschele and Fred Mitschele were directors of PVT at the
material times and that Malisa Phoiliang was a
de facto
director of PVT.

[
5
]

In the third action, which I will call PVT #1,
Action No. S081852, Vancouver Registry, PVT has sued Natco and its directors,
Raj Gurm, Hans Edblad and John Brainard.

[
6
]

The parties agree that these lawsuits should be
consolidated.  What is proposed, if any part of Natco’s claim is allowed to
stand, is that Natco will file a Consolidated Statement of Claim consolidating
the claims in Natco #1 and Natco #2, the form and substance of which will be
guided by the outcome of the current applications.  PVT will then advance all
of its defences and any counterclaims in response in the consolidated action.  By
consolidating all the claims, cross-claims and defences into Natco #1, this
will render the Natco #2 and PVT #1 actions redundant and they can then be
discontinued without costs.  This is a sensible way of avoiding a multiplicity
of proceedings.

[
7
]

Towards this end, at the hearing of these
applications Natco delivered to the Court a proposed Consolidated Statement of
Claim.  Counsel for Natco submitted that this Consolidated Statement of Claim was
a compromise attempt by Natco to deal with some of the defendants’ complaints.
Based on this submission, in considering this application I presumed that any
paragraphs of the Statements of Claim in Natco #1 and #2 that were not carried
forward into the draft Consolidated Statement of Claim were voluntarily
withdrawn from the pleadings and need not be addressed.

[
8
]

However, subsequent to the hearing of these
applications, Natco delivered to the Court a new version of the proposed
Consolidated Statement of Claim. This new draft pleading contains additional
paragraphs not in the previous version.  In my view, this further version of
pleadings is an additional submission by Natco after the hearing of the
application and a change in the position it took before me.  Natco should not
have submitted this new version without applying for leave to do so and
explaining its change in position.  Having failed to do so, I will not consider
Natco’s new submission. Any reference in these Reasons to the proposed
Consolidated Statement of Claim is to that version of the pleading relied on by
Natco at the hearing of this application, a copy of which was exhibited to the
Affidavit of Margaret Smith sworn July 25, 2008.

THE ALLEGED CLAIMS

[
9
]

Natco is a publically traded company, the shares
of which are traded on the OTC (Over the Counter) Bulletin Board in the United
States.

[
10
]

PVT is a company engaged in the business of
development and manufacture of automated parking meter equipment.

[
11
]

Natco claims that in or about November 2006,
Natco and PVT entered into discussions with the ultimate goal of a reverse
takeover of Natco by PVT.  A reverse takeover would enable the resulting
company to raise funds through the public stock market to manufacture and
market the automated parking meters.

[
12
]

Natco alleges it had two agreements with PVT.
First, Natco alleges that the parties signed a letter of intent on December 4,
2006, pursuant to which PVT agreed to a standstill clause that precluded it from
having discussions with third parties with respect to a sale of its shares or
assets for a defined period (the “Letter of Intent”).  The purpose of the
standstill clause was to allow PVT and Natco time to enter into negotiations
with respect to the proposed reverse takeover and time to conduct due
diligence.

[
13
]

The second agreement that Natco alleges it had
with PVT was a Letter of Agreement signed March 16, 2007, that set out certain
terms towards the goal of effecting a reverse takeover (the “Letter of Agreement”).
Natco claims it acted on the Letter of Agreement by loaning $1,485,000.00 (USD)
to PVT.  This was to be a loan of $2 million (USD), but the entire amount was
not advanced for reasons that are in dispute.

[
14
]

The substance of Natco’s claim seems to be that
it was induced to enter into the Letter of Agreement by the knowingly false
misrepresentations of PVT and PVT’s directors; that PVT subsequently breached
the terms of the Letter of Agreement in a variety of ways; and that PVT also
breached the Letter of Intent.  Natco seeks to recover the amounts loaned to
PVT and damages.

[
15
]

PVT alleges that Natco made false
representations to PVT and breached the Letter of Agreement by not advancing
the full $2 million loan, amongst other things, or, in the alternative, that
the Letter of Agreement was not binding as it was simply an agreement to
agree.  It says that any obligations owed to Natco under the Letter of
Agreement were conditional on the parties concluding a further agreement
described as an arrangement agreement, which never occurred.  It also claims
that Natco and its directors have defamed it.

THE RULE 18 SUMMARY TRIAL APPLICATION

[
16
]

In support of its Rule 18 summary trial
application, PVT says that if the Letter of Agreement was binding (which
remains an open question), it was terminated by Natco based on PVT’s insolvency.
PVT argues that a letter dated February 13, 2008 from counsel for Natco to
PVT’s counsel gave immediate notice of termination of the March 16, 2007 Letter
of Agreement on the basis that PVT was insolvent.  PVT says that Natco cannot
possibly prove that any breaches of the Letter of Agreement “caused” Natco to
lose the benefit of the Agreement.  Rather, Natco’s action in terminating the Letter
of Agreement is what caused Natco to lose the benefit of the Agreement from the
date of the termination forward. Therefore, PVT argues, Natco’s claim for loss
of the benefit of the contract should be dismissed.

[
17
]

Natco disagrees and says that the Letter of
Agreement had already been terminated or was fundamentally breached by PVT
before Natco’s counsel sent the letter of February 13, 2008.

[
18
]

As it turns out, this issue does not need to be resolved
on these applications because Natco conceded during the hearing of the
application that its theory of the case was that it would never have entered
into the Letter of Agreement had it known the truth about PVT (i.e. had the
alleged false representations not been made), and it was not seeking damages
for the loss of opportunity to benefit from the future performance of the Letter
of Agreement.  Natco has consented to dismissal of any claim for loss of
opportunity to profit from the Letter of Agreement and, in particular, for
“loss of opportunity to profit from the manufacture and marketing of the
Parking Equipment” as pleaded in its statement of claim in Natco #1 at para.
36(a), and in the proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim at para. 56(a).
This aspect of Natco’s claim will therefore be dismissed by consent.

REMAINING ISSUE ON RULE 18
APPLICATION

[
19
]

PVT asserts that Natco’s concession that it will
not advance a claim for the loss of opportunity to profit from the future
performance of the Letter of Agreement necessarily means that the remaining part
of Natco’s claim alleging damages for breaches of contract cannot be advanced
and must be struck as raising no triable issue. As such, the remaining issue
under PVT’s Rule 18 application is whether the Court ought to strike out those
parts of Natco’s claim dealing with alleged breach of the Letter of Agreement
on the basis that these allegations raise no triable issue.

[
20
]

In this regard, Natco pleads and relies on the Letter
of Agreement at paras. 19 through 35 of its statement of claim in Natco #1.  In
its pleading, Natco alleges that PVT breached the March 16, 2007 Letter of
Agreement by various actions and that it has suffered damages as a result.  Specifically,
it pleads at para. 36 of the Natco #1 statement of claim as follows:

36)      As a
result of the breach of the Agreement, Natco has suffered damages, including
inter
alia
:

(a)       loss of
opportunity to profit from the manufacture and marketing of the Parking
Equipment;

(b)       loss of sums
provided to PVT pursuant to the Agreement;

(c)        accounting
and other costs incurred to give effect to the Agreement;

(d)       decline in
the value of Natco shares, said decline causing millions of dollars in losses
to shareholders; and

(e)       legal costs.

[
21
]

As noted above, the claim for loss of
opportunity to profit under para. 36(a) of the statement of claim in Natco #1
has been dismissed by consent.

[
22
]

As well, Natco conceded on the hearing of this
motion that the relief sought in para. 36(d) of the statement of claim in Natco
#1 should also be struck, as a claim based on the decline in value of Natco
shares is not a claim that Natco can assert.  To the extent this aspect of
relief is repeated elsewhere in the claim, it should also be struck.  For
example, the following should all be struck: the last line of para. 126 reading
“[t]he shares of Natco have been subject to massive liquidation…”; the phrase
“the decline in value of Natco shares” in para. 127; and para. (d) of the
prayer for relief, “[d]amages from the decline in value of the shares of
Natco…”. These deletions from the Natco #1 statement of claim should be reflected
in any Consolidated Statement of Claim.

[
23
]

The claims in subparas. 36(b), (c) and (e) of
the statement of claim in Natco #1 are Natco’s claims for damages it incurred
in reliance on the Letter of Agreement.  Counsel for PVT argued that Natco’s
concession that it is not seeking damages for loss of opportunity to profit
from the contract with PVT meant that all of Natco’s claims based on breach of
contract must fail.

[
24
]

A party relying on Rule 18 is asserting that
there is no triable issue of fact to be determined and that the court may therefore
decide the issue as a matter of law.  The party resisting a summary judgment
application does not need to persuade the court that it will succeed on the
issues, but only that there is an issue for trial.

[
25
]

The summary judgment rule has been described as
serving an important purpose in the justice system, as it weeds out claims that
have no opportunity of success.  As stated by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Papaschase
Indian Band No. 136 v. Canada (Attorney General)
,
2008 SCC 14
, [2008] 5
W.W.R. 195 [
Papaschase
] at para.
10
:

The summary
judgment rule serves an important purpose in the civil litigation system.  It
prevents claims or defences that have no chance of success from proceeding to
trial.  Trying unmeritorious claims imposes a heavy price in terms of time and
cost on the parties to the litigation and on the justice system.  It is
essential to the proper operation of the justice system and beneficial to the
parties that claims that have no chance of success be weeded out an early
stage.  Conversely, it is essential to justice that claims disclosing real issues
that may be successful proceed to trial.

[
26
]

The Supreme Court of Canada commented on the
nature of the summary judgment rule in
Papaschase

at para.
11
, setting
out the following points:

(a)       The defendant
who seeks summary dismissal bears the evidentiary burden of showing that there
is “no genuine issue of material facts requiring trial”;

(b)       The
defendant must prove this; it cannot rely on mere allegations or the pleadings;

(c)        If the
defendant does prove this, the plaintiff must either refute or counter the
defendant’s evidence, or risk summary dismissal;

(d)       Each side
must “put its best foot forward with respect to the existence or non-existence
of material issues to be tried;”’

(d)       The chambers
judge may make inferences of fact based on the undisputed facts before the
court as long as the inferences are strongly supported by the facts.

[Formatting changed
from the original; citations omitted]

[
27
]

I do not accept PVT’s argument that Natco’s
remaining claims for breach of contract damages raise no triable issues.  While
Natco’s primary position is that it would not have entered into the contract
but for the fraudulent misrepresentations of the defendants, Natco is entitled
to advance in the alternative a claim for breach of contract.  Natco’s claim in
subparas 36(b), (c) and (e) of Natco #1 seems to be that it suffered damages in
the form of monies it advanced and expenses it incurred in reliance on the
contract subsequently breached by PVT.  Natco has filed sufficient evidence to
raise a triable issue.  This is properly an alternative to Natco’s claim that
it suffered damages in reliance on the misrepresentations by the defendants and
raises a triable issue.  However, Natco needs to properly set out that the
breach of contract claim for damages is an alternative claim to its claim based
on misrepresentation.

THE RULE 19(24) APPLICATIONS

[
28
]

The remaining motions brought by the parties
defending Natco’s claims seek to strike out all or part of Natco’s Statements
of Claim in Natco #1 and Natco #2 on the basis that they fail to disclose a
reasonable claim or, alternatively, are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous,
vexatious, or may prejudice, embarrass or delay the proceeding, or are an abuse
of process.  The defendants rely on Rule 19(24) and acknowledge that in order
to succeed they must establish that it is “plain and obvious” that the
pleadings suffer from one of the purported deficiencies:
Hunt v. Carey
Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959,
74 D.L.R. (4th) 321
;
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 CPC
(4
th
) 266 (BCSC),
B.C.J. No. 2160 [
Citizens
for Foreign Aid
]
.

[
29
]

The defendants also seek, in the alternative, an
order requiring Natco to provide particulars of some of its claims.

[
30
]

The issues on the Rule 19(24) application are:

(a)       Is it plain and obvious that
all or part of Natco’s statements of claim disclose no reasonable claims?

(b)       Is it plain and obvious that
all or part of Natco’s statements of claim are unnecessary, scandalous,
frivolous, vexatious, or may prejudice, embarrass or delay the proceeding, or
are an abuse of process?

(c)        If there are deficiencies in
Natco’s statements of claim, what order should the Court make to cure those
deficiencies?

Is it plain and obvious that all or part of Natco’s
Statements of Claim disclose no reasonable claims?

[
31
]

All of the causes of action being advanced by Natco
against each of the defendants are not readily apparent on first or even on second
reading of the Natco Statements of Claim. However, at the Court’s request, Natco
identified in its submissions that it is advancing the following causes of
action:  breach of contract by PVT; misrepresentation and deceit by PVT and PVT’s
directors; intentional interference with contractual relations by PVT’s
directors; and, “breach of fiduciary duty -- unjust enrichment -- remedial
constructive trust” in relation to PVT’s directors.

[
32
]

The question I must address for each of these
causes of action is whether or not it is plain and obvious that the claim in
its present form, or as amended, discloses no reasonable claim:
Kripps
v. Touche Ross & Co.
(1992),
1992 CanLII 923 (BC CA)
, 94 D.L.R. (4th) 284 (BCCA) at 289,
69 B.C.L.R. (2d) 62
.

Breach of Contract

[
33
]

The breach of contract claim as pleaded by Natco
against PVT does disclose a reasonable claim:  agreements are pleaded and so
are breaches of those agreements.  However, the drafting of the Natco statements
of claim is sloppy.  Some terms are capitalized as if defined, yet are not
defined, while other terms are defined, but the defined term is not used (see
for example, para. 19 of statement of claim in Natco #1, defining the “Letter
Agreement” but then using the term “Agreement” in the same paragraph and
throughout the pleading; para. 38 and various other paragraphs of Natco #1 referring
to “Patents” which are not defined).

[
34
]

It is also difficult to discern from Natco’s
statements of claim what actions are alleged to be in breach of which agreement
or agreements.

[
35
]

Furthermore, Natco’s statements of claim suffer
from superfluous pleadings of evidence.  Natco pleads multiple examples of evidence
of the alleged breach of the obligation to provide audited financial statements,
including evidence surrounding requests for financial statements, none of which
belong in a pleading.  See paras. 51(a), 52 to 77of the statement of claim in Natco
#1, which are redundant or irrelevant given that Natco has earlier pleaded at
para. 26 that PVT agreed to prepare audited financial statements, and at para.
33 (d) that PVT breached this agreement.  Rule 19(24)(1) requires pleading of
material facts and not the evidence by which these facts are to be proved.  While
Natco’s pleading in relation to breach of contract does disclose a reasonable
claim, Natco needs to cull the pleading of evidence from its statements of
claim.

Misrepresentation and
Deceit

[
36
]

The cause of action in misrepresentation and
deceit appears to be based on pleadings that allege that PVT and its directors,
including Fred Mitschele, made representations which Natco relied upon to its detriment
(para. 12, Natco #1) and that Fred Mitschele made untrue representations
concerning his prior business experience, achievements and work history (para.
85, Natco #1).  These pleadings are deficient in that they do not meet the
requirements of Rule 19(11) which requires particulars of any pleading of
misrepresentation.  The statement of claim in Natco #1 does not plead what was
said; when it was said; who said it; to whom it was said; whether or not it was
untrue; whether it was negligently or fraudulently said; and how it was relied
upon by Natco to its detriment.  These material facts need to be pleaded by Natco
to support any claim based on fraudulent or negligent misrepresentation or
deceit, in order that the defendants may know the case they have to meet.

[
37
]

The statement of claim in Natco #2 has the same
deficiencies regarding alleged representations of PVT and its directors:  see for
example paras. 24 and 25.

[
38
]

The proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim
refers to representations at paras. 30, 31, and perhaps misrepresentation by
omission at para. 59.  These proposed pleadings also fail to meet the
requirement of providing particulars, as required by Rule 19(11).

[
39
]

For any claim based on fraudulent or negligent
misrepresentation, Natco needs to plead specifically: who said what to whom;
when; whether what was said was untrue; what was wrong with what was said (to clarify,
for example, whether Natco is alleging it was said fraudulently or negligently);
and how Natco relied upon any statements to its detriment.  These particulars
should form part of any Consolidated Statement of Claim.  Since the
deficiencies in the pleading can be corrected by amendment, I am unable to
conclude that there is no reasonable cause of action in misrepresentation.

[
40
]

The statement of claim in Natco #2 alleges
additional representations were made by PVT but these appear to be to other
parties unconnected to Natco and these are not linked to any claim by Natco,
namely representations by PVT: concerning its strategic partnership with IBM
(paras. 39, 40); concerning the credentials of Malisa Phoiliang (para. 68); to
other investors (para. 69); and regarding an installation of parking meters in
Niagara Falls, New York (para. 71).  These representations are not the
foundation for any cause of action by Natco as presently pleaded and so are
“unnecessary” and should be struck pursuant to Rule 19(24)(b).

Intentional Interference
With Contractual Relations

[
41
]

The next cause of action asserted by Natco is
intentional interference with contractual relations by the defendant directors
of PVT, namely, Fred Mitschele, Mike Minor, and Jason Mitschele.  The pleading
of this cause of action is founded on the proposition that the directors of PVT
caused PVT to breach the Letter of Agreement with Natco, and that they

did
so in bad faith and outside the normal and ordinary scope of their employment
with PVT (para. 34 of the statement of claim in Natco #1 and para. 27 of the
statement of claim in Natco #2).

[
42
]

The defendants argue that because a company acts
through its directors, no cause of action can lie against the directors for
intentional interference with contractual relations when a company breaches a
contract, unless it is established that the directors’ dominating concern was
to deprive the opposite party of its contractual benefits.  Since here Natco
has pleaded that the purpose of the breach of contract was to achieve goals
which on their face would be for the benefit of PVT, the defendants argue that
there can be no separate claim against the directors for intentional
interference with contractual relations.

[
43
]

The defendants rely on two cases in support of the
proposition they advance:
Imperial Oil Ltd. v. C & G Holdings Ltd.

(1989),
1989 CanLII 3966 (NL CA)
, 62 D.L.R. (4
th
) 261 (Nfld. CA),
78 Nfld. & P.
E.I.R. 1
[
Imperial Oil
]

and
Digital.Doc Services (Canada) Inc. v. Future Shop Ltd.
,

[1997] B.C.J. No. 1689 [
Digital.Doc
]
,

which
adopted and relied on
Imperial Oil
.

[
44
]

In
Imperial Oil
,
the
Newfoundland Court of Appeal considered an appeal from a decision of a trial
judge dismissing a claim against directors for inducing breach of contract by a
company which had repudiated an agreement with the plaintiff.  The court
dismissed the appeal, and in so doing, commented on the applicability of the
tort of inducing breach of contract to the actions of a company director.  The court
noted that the duties of directors to a company have to be taken into account
in considering whether a director can be liable for inducing the breach of a
company’s contract.  It has to be kept in mind that a director of a company
owes fiduciary duties to the company.  A director may be obliged, in order to
fulfill his duties to the company, to cause the company to break a contract
where the director considers that the interests of the company may be served by
breaking the contract.  This means the scope of liability for inducing breach
of contract may be narrower for a director than it is for other persons.

[
45
]

However, the court in
Imperial Oil

did not say that a director may never

be liable for inducing breach of contract.  The
court noted that the law “does not go that far” (at p. 264).  Rather, the
question posed in
Imperial Oil
(at p. 265) was: in what
circumstances is a director who is not acting
bona fide
in the company’s
best interests liable for inducing a breach of contract by the company?  The
court held that even where a director is not acting
bona fide
, there
must exist some additional factor to justify a finding of intentional
interference with contractual relations.  The additional factor required to
justify liability is “affirmative proof that the dominating purpose of the
director’s act was aimed at depriving the aggrieved party of the benefits of
the contract” (at p. 266).

[
46
]

I do not read
Imperial Oil
as
laying down a strict test for when a director may be liable for inducing a
company’s breach of contract.  Rather, the court was clear to point out that
liability will depend on the circumstances and, in considering the
circumstances, the court must consider the individual director’s duty to the
company as a factor weighing against liability, as stated at p. 267:

Company directors
may, therefore, incur liability for instigating a breach of contractual
obligations by the company whose affairs they are directing.  That liability
will, however, have to be weighed against the individual director’s duty to the
company
and will depend on the circumstances of each case
.

[Emphasis added]

[
47
]

This court considered and applied
Imperial
Oil
in
Digital.Doc Services
.  In
Digital.Doc
Services
, the court concluded that the claims against the defendant
directors for inducing breach of an employment contract disclosed no reasonable
cause of action and were bound to fail. However, in
Digital.Doc Services,

the question was whether the defendant directors, acting within the
scope of

employment and acting in good
faith, could be liable for inducing breach of contract by the company.  This is
distinguishable from the present case, in which Natco is alleging that the
defendant directors were acting outside the scope of employment and in bad
faith.

[
48
]

On the pleadings, I am unable to conclude that Natco’s
claims against the individual directors for wrongfully inducing breach of
contract have no chance of success.  While the legal authorities make it clear
that it will be difficult to succeed in such a claim, I cannot conclude that
such a claim is bound to fail.

[
49
]

The defendants argue in addition that if Natco
is to allege that the directors were acting in bad faith, outside the normal
and ordinary scope of their employment as presently pleaded, then Natco should provide
particulars explaining in what way

the
directors’ actions were in bad faith and outside the scope of employment.  As I
read Natco’s statements of claim, it simply asserts that the directors’
directions to PVT to breach the agreement (presumably the Letter of Agreement)
were made in bad faith.  This is a conclusion which will be the subject of
evidence and argument, and I do not see that it needs further particulars.

Breach of
Fiduciary Duty

[
50
]

The next cause of action asserted by Natco is
described by Natco’s counsel as a claim against the directors of PVT for
“breach of fiduciary duty --unjust enrichment -- remedial constructive trust”.

[
51
]

In the statement of claim in Natco #1, Natco
pleads at paragraphs 78 and 79:

78)      PVT is
and was insolvent. PVT had financial statements that did not provide proper
understanding [
sic
] of the financial affairs of the company PVT.  The
directors of PVT, including the Defendant Fred Mitschele are personally liable
as, among other things, they allowed investors and lenders to invest, and lend
to PVT at a time when:

(a)       The true and
accurate financial position of the company was not known the directors [
sic
]
as the financial statements were not complete and accurate;

(b)       The company
was insolvent at the time investors made investment [
sic
] in PVT, and,
at the time lenders made loans to PVT.  These lenders include the Plaintiff
Natco.

79)      Further,
in addition to being liable to the lenders and investors, the directors of PVT,
including the Defendant Fred Mitschele, owed a fiduciary duty to the lenders
and investors from the time that PVT became insolvent.

[
52
]

In the statement of claim in Natco  #2, Natco
pleads at paragraph 36:

36)      Further,
in addition to being liable to the lenders and investors, the directors of PVT
including Mike Minor and Jason Mitschele owed a fiduciary duty to the lenders
and investors from the time that PVT became insolvent.

[
53
]

The above pleadings are inadequate to inform the
defendants of any basis for Natco alleging that the directors of PVT owed a
fiduciary duty to it, that the directors breached the fiduciary duty, and that
unjust enrichment or a constructive trust results therefrom.  As well, the allegations
regarding Natco’s liability to other lenders and investors are irrelevant and
unnecessary.

[
54
]

Natco’s attempted fix of this confusing pleading
is set out at para. 30 of its proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim:

30)      The
Directors of PVT knew, when entering into the Agreement that PVT was
insolvent.  They misrepresented the solvency of PVT to Natco in order to induce
Natco to enter into the Agreement and provide loans to PVT.  PVT and its
Directors misrepresented to Natco that PVT had the financial integrity to allow
for the creation of audited financial statements as required by investors and
the United States Federal Regulators so as to allow the RTO to complete.  The
Directors of PVT owed a fiduciary duty to Natco in these circumstances to
consider the interest of Natco in undertaking actions on behalf of PVT, and to act
in a manner which is not oppressive or unfairly prejudicial to Natco’s
interests.  The Directors of PVT owed, in that context, a duty of care to
Natco.  They breached this fiduciary duty in a number of ways, including, but
not limited to, failing to advise Natco that PVT was, at all relevant times,
insolvent when Natco was being induced by PVT and its Directors to become a
creditor of PVT.

[
55
]

The failure to advise Natco of the insolvency of
PVT in the circumstances when Natco was to become a creditor of PVT appears to
be the essence of the breach of fiduciary duty claim.  Natco seems to suggest
in the proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim that the breach of fiduciary
duty claim is based on the notion that the directors of PVT knew that PVT was
insolvent when entering into the Letter of Agreement with Natco, misrepresented
the solvency of PVT in order to induce Natco to enter into the Letter of
Agreement and, in the circumstances where Natco was to become a creditor of
PVT, had a fiduciary duty to Natco to advise it that PVT was insolvent.  The
fiduciary duty may also be informed by the allegation that the directors of PVT
personally benefited from the funds advanced by Natco to PVT, as alleged at
paras. 44, 45 and 46 of the proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim.

[
56
]

The defendant directors say that at law
directors owe fiduciary duties to the corporation only and not to creditors,
and therefore the claim that the Natco directors owed fiduciary duties to PVT
must be dismissed pursuant to Rule 19(24)(a).  The defendant directors say this
argument is supported by the case of
Peoples Department Stores Inc. v.
Wise
(2004),
2004 SCC 68 (CanLII)
,
3 S.C.R. 461
,
244 D.L.R. (4
th
)
564 [
Peoples Department Stores
], where the Supreme Court of
Canada held that directors of a company did not owe a duty to creditors.
However,
Peoples Department Stores
was dealing simply with the
scope of the statutory fiduciary duty owed by directors to their corporations
pursuant to s. 122(1)(a) of the
Canada Business Corporations Act
:
see paras. 37, 42, 43.  The
Peoples Department Stores
decision does
not stand for the proposition that a director of a company that is insolvent will
never owe a common law fiduciary duty to a creditor.

[
57
]

Counsel for the defendant directors focused on
the statutory fiduciary duty of directors in challenging Natco’s pleadings and
cited no authority for the proposition that a director could never owe a
fiduciary duty to a creditor at common law.  Whether or not a fiduciary duty
exists in certain circumstances will turn on the facts of the relationship
between the parties.  In
K.L.B. v. British Columbia
,
2003 SCC 51 (CanLII)
, [2003] 2 S.C.R.
403,
230 D.L.R. (4th) 513
, the Supreme Court
of Canada reviewed the case law and noted that typically fiduciary relationships
involve loyalty, discretionary power and trust, and “the avoidance of a
conflict of duty and interest and a duty not to profit at the expense of the
beneficiary”: at para. 49, citing
Lac Minerals Ltd. v. International
Corona Resources Ltd.
,
1989 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 574,
61 D.L.R. (4th) 14
[
Lac Minerals
]
.

[
58
]

Counsel for the defendants referred to the case
of
Jam’s International Ventures Ltd. v. Westbank Holdings Ltd.
,
2002
BCSC 1788
,
B.C.J. No. 2894 [
Jam’s
International
]
,

where
an application to add a director as a defendant was refused.  The lawsuit
involved a dispute between two corporations.  The plaintiffs applied to add a
claim that the proposed defendant director of the opposite company had breached
a fiduciary duty owed to the plaintiffs.  The court in
Jam’s
International
noted that there was no evidence to support the
plaintiff’s claim that the director owed the plaintiffs a fiduciary duty and had
breached that duty, and no evidence to indicate that he had

acted in any capacity other than as alter ego and
controlling mind of the defendant company.

[
59
]

Jam’s International
is not on point because, unlike an application under Rule
19(24)(a),

evidence was required on that
application to add a party, and so the court reached its conclusion after
weighing the evidence.  On the present application pursuant to Rule 19(24)(a),
evidence is not admissible when considering whether the plaintiff is advancing
a reasonable claim.  Furthermore, Natco has pleaded that the directors were
acting in bad faith outside the scope of employment.  While this is a fact
pleaded to support the claim of intentional interference with contractual
relations, it is also a fact which may come into play on the breach of
fiduciary duty claim.  This allegation distinguishes the case from
Jam’s
International
.

[
60
]

Counsel for Natco cited J. P. Sarra and R. B.
Davis,
“Director and Officer Liability in Corporate Insolvency”

(Toronto:  Butterworths Canada, 2002), as support for the claim that directors
may owe fiduciary duties to creditors. It should be noted that these authors
were in part relying on the trial decision in
Peoples Department Stores

which was subsequently overturned.  Nevertheless, these authors argued that
there may be strong policy reasons for finding that directors of insolvent
corporations owe duties to creditors.  This suggests that there is room at
common law for concluding that a director of an insolvent company owes a duty
to creditors.

[
61
]

I am unable to conclude that it is plain and
obvious that a claim cannot succeed on the basis that the directors of PVT owed
and breached a fiduciary duty to Natco, a creditor of PVT.  However, para. 30
of the proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim is deficient in that:  it does
not define the “Directors”, although counsel for Natco confirmed this is meant
to apply to Fred Mitschele, Mike Minor and Jason Mitschele; it does not define the
“United States Federal Regulators”; it confuses duty of care (a negligence
concept) with breach of fiduciary duty; and it fails to plead the material
facts of all alleged breaches of fiduciary duty, stating that the fiduciary
duty was breached “in a number of ways, including, but not limited to, failing
to advise Natco that PVT was, at all relevant times, insolvent…”.     The
defendant directors are entitled to know the case they have to meet and this
means Natco must plead every alleged breach of fiduciary duty and must not
advance general allegations based on the phrase “including but not limited to”.
The breach of fiduciary duty claim should therefore be amended.

Remedial Constructive
Trust/Unjust Enrichment

[
62
]

Natco says that it has re-drafted its
constructive trust claim at para. 45 of its proposed Consolidated Statement of
Claim.  The thrust of this claim appears to be that the defendant directors of
PVT, Fred Mitschele, Mike Minor and Jason Mitschele, and the defendant Malisa
Phoiliang (alleged earlier in the pleading to be a
de facto
director of
PVT), each have received some of the funds advanced by Natco to PVT and that
this was always their purpose.  Paragraph 45 of the proposed Consolidated
Statement of Claim reads:

45.  PVT and its
Directors and Phoiliang never intended to complete the RTO contemplated by the
Agreement.  Rather they intended to utilize the funds advanced by Natco for
personal purposes, those purposes including, but not limited to,

(a)       marketing
of the Parking Technologies; and

(b)       obtaining
funds personally from the investment by Natco in PVT.

PVT and its
Directors, to the extent that they have any interest in the Parking
Technologies, or have personally taken funds from Natco’s investment in PVT,
hold them in trust for Natco.  PVT and its Directors have been unjustly
enriched by the receipt of Sums from Natco. The Plaintiff claims a remedial
constructive trust.

[
63
]

A constructive trust is an equitable remedy sometimes
founded on principles of unjust enrichment and at other times founded on good
conscience.  It is a remedy which can be used to trace proceeds of fraud or
even proceeds of breach of fiduciary duty.  Here I understand the allegations
against PVT and the defendant directors to be that they knowingly participated
in a fraud (the fraudulent misrepresentations of PVT’s solvency) and breach of
fiduciary duty (failure to warn of PVT’s insolvency), and then to the extent
they received proceeds of the fraud and breach of fiduciary duty, these proceeds
are traceable by the equitable remedy of constructive trust.  These are causes
of action which are legally available:  Peter D. Maddaugh & John D. McCamus,

Law of
Restitution
looseleaf ed. (Aurora, ON:  Canada Law
Book Inc., 2004), 2-1 to 2-21;
see also
Pettkus v. Becker
,
1980 CanLII 22 (SCC)
, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 834,
117 D.L.R. (3d) 257
;

Lac Minerals
;

Sorochan v. Sorochan

1986 CanLII 23 (SCC)
,
[1986] 2 S.C.R.
38
,
[1987] 74 A.R. 67
;
Peter v. Beblow

1993 CanLII 126 (SCC)
,
[1993] 1 S.C.R. 980
,
101 D.L.R. (4th) 621
;
Martindale
Estate v. Martindale
(1998)
1998 CanLII 4561 (BC CA)
,
162 D.L.R. (4
th
) 475 (BCCA)
,
55 B.C.L.R. (3d) 63
;
Korkontzilas v. Soulos

1997 CanLII 346 (SCC)
,
[1997] 2 S.C.R. 217
,

146 D.L.R. (4
th
)
214
.

[
64
]

The constructive trust/unjust enrichment pleading
in the proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim is deficient.  It is very
confusing.  It uses capitalized terms as if defined, which are not defined
elsewhere; it raises the concept of the defendants’ intent but does not say
there was anything wrongful about this intent; it refers to unjust enrichment
but not a corresponding deprivation.  However, despite its flaws, if it was
amended properly, I am unable to conclude that it is plain and obvious that the
claim to impose the remedy of constructive trust, as against PVT or the
defendant directors, over monies they have received from Natco’s advance to PVT
or proceeds of those monies, is bound to fail.

[
65
]

The prayer for relief in the statement of claim in
Natco #1 also seeks in para. (e) a declaration that the assets and patents of
PVT are held in trust for Natco (this is carried forward to para. (i) of the
prayer for relief in the proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim).  Natco’s
claim to a trust over the assets and patents of PVT appears to be based on a
claim to a resulting trust and constructive trust resulting from the $1.485
million (USD) advanced by Natco to PVT.  Natco alleges the money was advanced
under a common intention that from that point on the property held by PVT was
held in trust for Natco; and that the money was used to enhance the value of
the PVT assets and the patents:  paras. 57 and 58, proposed Consolidated
Statement of Claim.  I am unable to say that such a claim in respect of PVT’s
assets is bound to fail, on the pleadings.

[
66
]

However, nowhere in the pleadings is it alleged
that PVT itself owns any patents.  The claim in subpara. (e) of the prayer for
relief in the statement of claim in Natco #1 that PVT holds its “Patents”
(undefined) in trust for Natco, is not supported by the pleadings.  Rather,
Natco alleges that certain directors of PVT hold all relevant patents.  The
claims in subparas. (f) and (g) of the prayer for relief in Natco #1, that the
defendant directors of PVT hold patents as bare trustees for the benefit of
Natco, and that the defendant directors and Malisa Phoiliang are trustees
de
son tort
, are also not supported by the pleadings in the existing or the
proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim.

[
67
]

If the concept is that the money obtained by PVT
from Natco was on the basis of fraud or breach of fiduciary duty and that this
money then ended up in others hands or in other assets, there may be a basis
for a claim for the equitable remedy of constructive trust.  However, the claim
as presently pleaded does not provide enough material facts to support such a
remedy against the “Patents”.  There are no material facts pleaded which would
explain a basis for alleging that the monies advanced by Natco to PVT enhanced
pre-existing patents owned by others; nor are there material facts pleaded
which would explain a basis for alleging the conclusion that the individual
defendants are “trustees
de son tort
”.As such, subparas. (f) and (g)  in
the prayer for relief in the statement of claim in Natco #1 must either be
struck out, or the pleadings amended to provide material facts to support these
remedies.

[
68
]

The claim by Natco against Malisa Phoiliang is
different than that against the other individual defendants.  She was not a
director, but she is alleged to be a
de facto
director of PVT.  Yet
nothing flows from this in the pleadings.

[
69
]

There are some allegations regarding Ms. Phoiliang
that have no apparent relevance, namely:  that she is the “right hand man” of Fred
Mitschele (para. 5 of proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim); that she was
responsible for maintaining the share register of PVT and failed to do so
properly (paras. 47 and 52 of proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim); that
she and Fred Mitschele took certain steps to cause employees and agents of PVT
to contact shareholders of PVT to coerce them into saying they were accredited
investors (para. 51, proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim); and that she
knew that the failure to keep an accurate share register and the sale of shares
contrary to law made it impossible for Natco and PVT to complete the proposed
RTO (para. 55, proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim).  These do not found
any cause of action against her.  She is not alleged to have made any
misrepresentations to Natco, or owed or breached a fiduciary duty to Natco, nor
is it alleged that Natco relied on her in any way (unlike the allegations
against the other personal defendants).

[
70
]

Natco also pleads at para. 45 of the proposed
Consolidated Statement of Claim that Ms. Phoiliang “never intended to complete
the RTO contemplated by the Agreement”.  This is irrelevant and unnecessary, as
nowhere is it pleaded that she made any representations to induce Natco to
enter into an agreement nor is she party to any agreement with Natco.

[
71
]

In the rest of para. 45 and at para. 46 of the
proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim, Natco alleges that Ms. Phoiliang may
have received funds from Natco’s investment in PVT.  Perhaps here is the nub of
a claim against Ms. Phoiliang:  that she received proceeds of fraud or of
breach of fiduciary duty.  However the pleading is difficult to follow and if
this is alleged, it needs to be clearly set out.

[
72
]

Based on the existing pleadings and proposed
Consolidated Statement of Claim, I conclude there is no reasonable claim
against Malisa Phoiliang other than the possible claim that she has received
proceeds of fraud or proceeds of breach of fiduciary duty, over which Natco
seeks to have the court impose the remedy of a constructive trust.  Such a claim
would need to be clarified to make it clear whether it is based on the
allegation that she is an innocent recipient of the alleged proceeds of fraud
or proceeds of breach of fiduciary duty, or is based on the allegation that she
knowingly assisted in the wrongful acts or knowingly received proceeds of the
wrongful acts.  If Natco alleges that she knowingly participated in wrongful
acts, particulars must be pleaded of Ms. Phoiliang’s participation.

Is it plain and obvious that all or part of Natco’s
Statements of Claim are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, vexatious, or may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the proceeding, or are an abuse of process?

[
73
]

A pleading is unnecessary or embarrassing if it
is so confusing that it is difficult to understand what is being pleaded, or if
it does not advance any claim known to law, or is irrelevant to the real issues
in dispute between the parties:  see
Isaac v. Guardian Capital Group
,

2004 BCSC 254
,
B.C.J. No. 360
;
Citizens
for Foreign Aid
;
Gittings v. Caneco Audio-Publishers Inc.

(1987),
1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (BCSC
)
,
1988 Carswell BC 194
;
Kiddie
v. Dumas Hotels Ltd.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 (CA).

[
74
]

It is plain and obvious that large parts of the
original Natco Statements of Claim are unnecessary or embarrassing.

[
75
]

The pleadings allege conduct on the part of the
defendants which is not at all linked to any cause of action on the part of
Natco.  In this regard, I have already referred to some irrelevant pleadings
against Malisa Phoiliang.  As other examples, Natco pleaded at para. 5 of the
statement of claim in Natco #2 that “Malisa Phoiliang is illegally working in
Canada”.  This pleading is not linked to any cause of action by Natco and on
its face can be for no other purpose other than to attempt to discredit Ms.
Phoiliang.

[
76
]

Natco has many irrelevant pleadings in Natco #1
and Natco #2 dealing with PVT’s relationships with other parties (for example,
IBM and investors).  These are unnecessary as they are not linked to any cause
of action against the defendants.

[
77
]

Despite the purported attempt to improve upon
its earlier pleadings, Natco’s proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim still
suffers from pleading many apparently irrelevant facts, arguments and evidence.
For example, at para. 41 of the proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim, Natco
purports to set out particulars of PVT’s breach of its contractual obligation
to provide financial statements and other documents. The examples at subparas. 41(a)
and (b) make no sense as they are introduced as particular examples of a breach
of contract, but they merely repeat asserted terms of contract without setting
out the breach.  Subparagraph 41(d) is fine only in the first half of the first
sentence reading “[t]he financial statements were never produced by PVT.”  But
the rest of para. 41(d) contains argumentative and irrelevant statements that
“the Defendant Fred Mitschele employed a litany of obstructionism and stall
tactics regarding the financial statements of PVT.”  The last sentence of para.
41(d) states that “[t]he other two directors of PVT, Mike Minor and Jason
Mitschele failed to have PVT comply with the material terms of the March 16,
2007 Letter of Agreement”.  This allegation is irrelevant, since nowhere is it
pleaded that these directors owed an independent positive duty to Natco to
cause PVT to comply with its contractual obligations.

[
78
]

There are many more examples of irrelevant
pleadings in Natco’s statements of claim and proposed Consolidated Statement of
Claim.  For example, Natco pleads at paras. 50 through 54 of the proposed
Consolidated Statement of Claim certain facts that suggest PVT and its
directors were in some way violating securities laws.  This then is followed by
the confused para. 55, which pleads that failures by PVT and the directors and
Malisa Phoiliang constitute breach of agreement (the only agreement is with
PVT, so how are the actions of the individuals relevant?) and pleads
misrepresentation and concealment without any particulars of what was the representation
or duty to disclose.

[
79
]

Many paragraphs of the Natco statements of claim
and the proposed Consolidated Statement of Claim contain multiple facts,
evidence and argument.

[
80
]

Further, many paragraphs of the Natco Statements
of Claim are confusing. For example, the claim by Natco for “an accounting as
against the Directors of PVT and PVT” does not make sense:  para. 107,
statement of claim, Natco #1.  The claim does not state what Natco seeks an
accounting of:  is it an accounting of what happened to Natco’s money?  Is it
an accounting for profits?  The plaintiff did not point out in argument what
cause of action supports this claim for accounting.

[
81
]

The purpose of pleadings is to enable the other
side to know the case it has to meet; and to inform the trial judge of the real
issues in the case.  As noted by Madam Justice Southin, when a plaintiff files
“a hopelessly inadequate statement of claim, there is nothing upon which the
trial judge can concentrate his or her mind”:
Cotton v. Wellsby

(1991),
1991 CanLII 5730 (BC CA)
, 59 B.C.L.R. (2d) 366 (CA), B.C.J. No. 2783 at para. 29.

[
82
]

Pleadings which are poorly written and
hopelessly confused, such as the Natco statements of claim, may be sustainable
on a Rule 19(24) application as disclosing a cause of action, but may
nonetheless create a very poor impression of the litigant’s case and as such
are not effective advocacy.  Parties should appreciate that what they set out
in a statement of claim or statement of defence is going to serve as a guideline
for analysis at the end of the trial as to whether that party proved its case
at trial.  By pleading evidence and irrelevant facts, perhaps so as to cast
aspersions on its opponents, a party is setting up a bigger burden for itself
at trial.  When it cannot prove the allegations, the party hoping to prejudice
the court against its opponents has only succeeded in undermining its own
credibility.

[
83
]

It is clear that the problems of irrelevant and
embarrassing pleadings, as is evident from the statements of claim in Natco #1
and Natco #2, have not been cured by Natco’s proposed Consolidated Statement of
Claim.  More work needs to be done by Natco to make this a proper pleading.

If there are deficiencies in Natco’s Statements of Claim,
what Order should the Court make to cure those deficiencies?

[
84
]

The court has numerous options open to it in
giving directions which have the overall goal of curing defects in a pleading.
One option is to give directions to amend specific paragraphs of a pleading.
Another option is to strike out the whole pleading with leave to file an
amended claim in accordance with directions of the court.  Yet another option,
one urged upon me by the defendants in this case, is to strike the whole
pleading with liberty to the plaintiff to apply to the court for leave to file
an amended pleading.  This latter option will put the plaintiff to the test of
justifying its new pleading before the court will allow it to be filed.

[
85
]

Here, given that there is a clear need to
consolidate Natco #1 and Natco #2, it is obvious that an entirely new Consolidated
Statement of Claim needs to be filed in any event, rather than piecemeal
amendments of Natco #1 and Natco #2.  However, the proposed Consolidated
Statement of Claim suffers from many of the same deficiencies as the original
statements of claim. It would be a monumental task for this Court to go through
each line of Natco’s pleading and give directions as to whether to strike a
sentence or amend it so that it meets the rules of pleadings.  That would amount
to the court re-writing the pleadings, which is not the court’s role.  I
conclude that it is better that Natco start fresh and draft and file an
entirely revised Consolidated Statement of Claim which takes into account these
Reasons and the rules concerning pleadings as set out in Rule 19.

[
86
]

I will order that Natco consolidate its claims
in Natco #2 and Natco #1 by filing a new consolidated pleading in Natco #1.  I
will expect Natco to remove irrelevant and confusing pleadings, to plead
material facts and not evidence or argument, and to provide more particulars and
material facts of its claims of misrepresentation and breach of fiduciary duty
and any trust claims.  However, if Natco’s new pleading remains deficient, the
defendants have their remedy in an application to this Court to strike all or
part of the new pleading.  In this regard, it should be kept in mind that some
leeway has to be given to a plaintiff in pleading its case, as noted by this Court
in
Carr v. Cheng
,
2007 BCSC 997
,
[2008]
B.C.W.L.D. 2384
.

[
87
]

In conclusion, I order as follows:

(a)       that the
claims of Natco for “loss of opportunity to profit from the manufacture and
marketing of the Parking Equipment” be dismissed, by consent;

(b)       that the
claims of Natco for “decline in value of Natco shares” be dismissed, by consent;

(c)        that
the actions Natco #1 and Natco #2 be consolidated;

(d)       that Natco
has leave to file a Consolidated Statement of Claim in Natco #1;

(e)       that the
claims of Natco in Natco #2 against Malisa Phoiliang be dismissed, with the
exception that Natco has leave to properly plead a claim for receipt of
proceeds of fraud or receipt of proceeds of breach of fiduciary duty and a
related constructive trust if this is what Natco alleges;

(f)         that if
Natco claims misrepresentation or breach of fiduciary duty or the existence of
any trust, or seeks a remedy in trust, that Natco must plead particulars of each
alleged misrepresentation and each breach of fiduciary duty and the material
facts which support any claims in trust; and,

(g)       that any
pleadings filed by the defendants in response to the Consolidated Statement of
Claim in Natco #1 consolidate all positions the defendants seek to properly
plead in Natco #1, Natco #2 and PVT #1.

[
88
]

If the parties wish to direct submissions to the
procedure for consolidation of all claims into Natco #1 and for discontinuing
the proceedings in Natco #2 and PVT #1, then they may bring an application
before me.
